sentences.text: Hey, Andy, how are you?
I'm good, thank you.
How you doing?
I'm doing well.
Thanks so much for taking the time and.
Sorry, it's taking us a few tries to get the timing right.
I know this always happens when we're across the pond from one another.
Yeah, it might be because Ahmed is in Asia as well, so probably got it.
Okay, that doesn't help.
Well, amazing.
And you're on Australian time, I think.
Sorry, are you based out of the UK?
Yeah, I'm based in the UK.
So we are in.
Yeah, we're.
We're on three continents, so we're in the US I would say the majority of our clients are US based, but about 95%.
So most of our work is in the US time zone, but we work here, buy and sell side and.
And we are head HQed in in the UK.
Amazing.
Amazing.
Can I ask one request before we get started?
I see you have fireflies on, or at least Ahmed does.
Would you be okay if he shared his notes after the call with me?
I have my own fireflies.
I can add in if that's easier, but.
Well, the more the merrier.
I wouldn't be offended.
I don't know if I've got direct access to all.
Maybe it's one, but.
Okay.
Then I'll add mine in as we get to know each other.
I'll do that as I'm giving my intro.
Well, great.
Andy.
Yeah.
I don't know how much I shared with Ahmed and how much he was able to share with you.

We're an early stage investment firm with a little bit of a unique model where not only can we fund startups that approach us seeking capital, but we can also proactively go out and launch new businesses ourselves if there's an opportunity to do so.
And if we determine that a new venture needs to be launched VR firm, there's then a couple of ways we'll actually go about doing that.
One is completely de novo.
Hiring an executive team, giving them equity, capitalizing them and.
And starting from complete scratch.

The other is hiring an executive team and helping them identify a 1, 2, 3 acquisitions to kind of form the base of this new business and jumpstart whatever opportunity we're doing and that the strategy in our portfolio is kind of a case by case basis.
There's sometimes where it made sense to start brand new de novo, other times where it makes sense to make an acquisition depending on multiples, depending on some other dynamics.
But this is one project where we're still in the relatively early days we, we do research and analysis.
Analysis that lasts somewhere between three, four months.
Typically we're still in kind of the month one to two range and so.

But all the dynamics we're hearing and all of the opportunities that have been kind of exposed to us via conversations experts make us think one, this is really interesting for a firm like ours and I can get into why in a minute.
But two, if we were to start something, it seems much more attractive to start with an acquisition or two or three than to have to jumpstart from scratch.
Start from scratch.
So that's a little bit of the context for this call.
Can get into more of the weeds there.
But happy to turn it over to you to hear more about your firm or also answer any questions you might have off the bat about us.
Yeah, great.
So we are an M and A advisory working on the buy and the sell side.
We work exclusively in marketing services.
We did until we made some acquisitions ourselves.
But certainly our experiences in marketing services and we like to say work on the buy and sell side.
Obviously you've come across Agencies co already, which is our marketplace for agencies to buy and sell.
And so that gives us obviously a good overview of the market and what's available.
Puts us in a lot of inboxes as well because of our outbound marketing.
And then we work on the buy side as capital A.
So we work with clients who are either private equity, private equity backed or private investors or agencies that are just going for it.
Sure.
They're making multiple acquisitions and growing through the ceiling within organic growth.
So yeah, get to see both sides of the table.
I'm pretty visible in the market as well.
There are obviously a lot of similar firms, but because of Agencies co and also I do a lot of social media so we get a lot of stuff coming to us.
Sure.
So yeah, I was really interested to see, and I'd love to find out what your reasons are for getting into marketing that you, you signed NDAs for multiple.
I did.
I wasn't sure if that was typical and I was, as I was doing it, I was saying, you know what, there's got to be a more efficient way to do this, so let's just get on the phone with someone.
Well, yeah, there possibly is, but what we do find is not many people do that.
So I would say most because of the way that marketing services work.
If they are not a similar or adjacent service provider, maybe they're just looking for scale or geography, then they tend to only apply for one or two.
Right.

Unless there's Certain types of buyers and when I see somebody applying for tons of stuff that either means they don't know what they're doing or they are, they're performing some kind of roll up themselves or they've got some strategy going.
The roll up is exactly it.
And yeah, I think, you know, part of the desire is to get under the hood on some of those opportunities.

I can tell you our basic criteria and I'm happy to get into the thesis of why half a million to 2 million ish of EBITDA maybe a little bit lower, you know and on the lower end we would probably be more interested in doing more deals, rolling up more of them.
So probably trying to start with 2 to 3 million total of EBITDA to get us started.
We typically want to see something along the lines of this 15 to 20% EBITDA margin.
You know, it seems like there are opportunities, especially on your website.
Others I've seen you can get margins up close to 25.
Some look like they're pushing 30, 35.
I'm sure they're doing something unique there to be able to do that.

So it feels like we have the opportunity to help grow the biggest ones obviously and this is where you can't get a sense of this just from the teaser, which is why I'm looking for the sim is comments around the sale, you know what, what factor of the team, which amount of the team is dedicated to outbound sales, new business development are.
We've done similar roll ups here in the short term rental space in a kind of a traditional home services business space.
We're working on one potentially in pest control.
And the thing that these businesses are really attractive to us is we feel really qualified to build portfolio level centers of excellence for lack of a better term, mainly doing sales.
A lot of the operational things.
We want to layer that on onto opportunities where we see hey, you've got a 10 person agency, the only person really doing new business development is the founder.

Can we complement that, can we keep the founder on board, incentivize them to stay along with us, obviously help maintain those client relationships for some period of time and kind of supercharge the sales effort to a degree with a combination of resources, shared resources and obviously technology.
And then I'm loathe to add this on though.

I think it is part of the thesis that we're obviously not unique here is can you implement significant AI or just more traditional technology even to make these less creative operations within an agency more efficient?
The sales, the onboarding, the customer Retention, the reporting and analytics, all things that I think are really important.
And you know, an agency of these sizes that we're talking about, more likely than not, hasn't dedicated a lot of time or attention to them.
And by bringing them into our roll up, we're able to do that, Help them do that.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, some good observations there.
So I'd say there's a couple of things straight off the bat.
What we tend to see is either really people heavy businesses, they then have the lower margins.

And I would say traditionally what buyers were looking for were sort of that 15 to 25% margin because it would usually indicate there was a layer of management which if the founder is going to get out, then you've still got a business to run once they've left.
But creative agencies in particular and some different types, they tend to be really people heavy and they're also, they are creatives.
So they tend to be a bit fluffy and very bad at firing people.
So as they hire, they keep people for like 15 years, even when they become useless.
So there's quite a lot of that involved.
And then the other thing is, in terms of the biz dev stuff, one thing that really perplexes me in the marketing industry is that nobody does marketing for themselves.
What they tend to do is they live off referrals.
And I kind of understand why.
Particularly if it's a lifestyle business, there's absolutely no harm in, you know, getting two or three clients a year and they've got enough to live on a couple of staff.
Right.
So there's that type.
But you see these companies accidentally grow because they're good and they never get beyond that.
So what happens is people move to different companies, they move to different brands and then they come back to the same agency over and over and they think that they're amazing because that happens.
They, they don't realize that they're actually killing their business because they do no marketing, no biz dev, no outbound sales, they don't do any content themselves.
Everything they tell their clients to do, they don't do for themselves.
So it does leave a huge opportunity for a buyer, especially in a roll up scenario.
Because if you can find one company that does do great marketing for themselves and a bunch of others that don't, then everybody shares whoever's got the engine.
But it sounds like you guys are strapping that to something else anyway.
Yeah, exactly.
We, I mean, we are.
Our structure is a little different than maybe the traditional lower middle market private equity firm.
We do have a Longer time horizon.
We're not looking to flip things in three to five years, probably closer to seven to 10 years typically.
And we really want to grow these opportunities, especially in this space.
You know, I'm loathed not mention the multiple arbitrage opportunity that appears to be here where it seems like it scales linearly.
Right.
You have single digit ebitda companies trading 3, 4, 5 times.
Feels like as you get closer to double digit ebitda, those multiples grow closer to double digit multiples.
And so, right.
If we can roll up 3 million of EBITDA, grow it over 5 years, double it at that of those entities, now we're at 6 million, layer on a couple of more acquisitions over that time, get to 10 million.
You know, suddenly we've turned whatever that if you know we're thinking an average acquisition, you tell me a 4 million, we turn $12 million into $100 million of equity.
There's obviously or enterprise value at least depending on how we leverage these, if they are financeable.
That's a really attractive, you know, and that's assuming everything goes perfectly, which it rarely does.
But just that story is very attractive to someone like this.
Yeah, totally.
And it's a really good opportunity for that.
And one of the things that really interests me about somebody like yourself that's kind of digging in for the first time is that we are actually putting roll ups together ourselves.
So we're finding companies that are around the 1 million EBITDA sort of ceiling, I guess I call it a ceiling where you would find a natural.
And these aren't necessarily bad agencies, but they've kind of hit a natural ceiling where their people don't really know how to get much bigger than that.
But combined you could take three to five, maybe a bit more even of these businesses.
And we're working with our team as well.
So we've got some COO and strategics from, well in fact managing directors from large agencies.
They're working with us to map that out.
But what we're not doing is acquiring them.
We're putting these together in groups and then selling them as a group.
Interesting.
Yeah.
Which could work for you.
What we were hoping to do because like you just said is if we can build a group between sort of 5 and 8 million EBITDA, we're getting much closer to double figures.
Single solo agencies would sell for probably around 5 times EBITDA.

Whereas if we get a bunch of between the 5 and 8 mark, they're much like to sell for 8 or 9 times multiple so we're putting these groups together and we're handing that money back to the founders really and taking a small cut ourselves.
So we have started building these groups.
We have a really interesting one in E commerce and we've got a couple in experiential or immersive experiences, which is really a really nice vertical to be in.
Interesting.
I mean a couple of things there.
One and right.
I'm a tourist into this world, so.
And I recognize the reasons for some of these dynamics to persist that I think are low hanging fruit for someone like us to ideally, you know, take advantage of a lot of these agencies.
They seem to, if they do have business development or account executives even, you know, they're both.
That person is both the hunter and the farmer, the gatherer.
Right.
So each person is responsible for $1 million book of business.
If you're at that million dollars, you're doing great.
You're not really incentivized to expand.
Whereas if you had all the resources in the world, right.
So then once that, once that representative whomever gets to a million dollars, they're kind of disincentivized from expanding beyond that.
Obviously there's commission, but their workload, right.
You're asking them to do two tasks simultaneously.
Go win new business while maintaining the relationships that already exist.
Whereas I'm sure there, I know there are agencies that already do do this, but strikes me every agency should do this, kind of segregate the responsibilities.
There's a person who goes out and you know, plants the seeds of new relationships.
Then you have the account executive who kind of takes over as that trusted contact brings them in house.
You have that dedicated person out there constantly growing the business.
This is more of a question than a statement.

I come to learn and correct if it's wrong that a lot of these agencies care less about churn, that's less of a KPI for them than they do about just logo or customer count growth and obviously revenue growth.
Right.
And so which is interesting, obviously the churn is an input into how much is my top line, how much are my customers growing.
But is there an opportunity to make an acquisition, reduce the churn, Discover why the churn is happening in diligence.
Reduce the churn while maintaining the growth.
Right.
And so you've kind of on a net basis supercharged growth because you've cut the churn in half and you maintain the growth.
You know, it looks like a much more hockey stick growth opportunity.
I wonder if those two are related in a lot of ways.
Yeah, I think they certainly don't manage their businesses as if they're like a SaaS business or a startup in the valley or whatever.
These guys do tend to go off feelings a lot.
I don't want to make it sound like they're too fluffy, but there does tend to be an irresponsibleness around the biz dev the maintenance of it.
They're quite happy for clients to move through and churn because it means they get more interesting opportunities.
Right.
So they will potentially kind of allow it to happen so that their work and their day and their team have interesting stuff to work on.
So there is definitely a sense of that because what I find is that they very rarely lock people down into any kind of contracts.
Even if somebody's been a client for like 10 years and is definitely coming back, it can be very loose and free the way that they work with people and they work on almost everything as a project.
So yeah, I mean it's a real.
It's really nice to find a proper, you know, well run agency with a ton of retainers in there which they exist but they are the unicorns I think.
But that's where the real opportunity lies is being able to lock that in.
And those tend to be run by the less creative agencies.
So the ones that do outbound marketing or those types of things, ABM is, is probably one of the the better categories where.

Well, just to play devil's advocate, funny enough, like for us again trying to think about arbitrage in a way we'd love to find an agency that has good bones but is missing some of that exactly as you described there.
They.
Maybe we're not looking for a unicorn.
We're looking for the ones that hey, we're.
They're missing these low hanging fruits, right?
They're letting customers churn on purpose to your point because they don't have the resources or they don't have the bandwidth to, to maintain those relationships.
Can we take off some of that workload via technology versus via centralized shared services?
Right.
And that unlocks more bandwidth for the agency level team.
I don't, I'd love to learn more about that topic you're about to get to I think which is like for our purposes, right.
Let's imagine we do have this portfolio leadership level in place.
I'm curious like and let's say, right, we want to be somewhat diversified.
We want to tackle one to three specializations.
Performance marketing, social media marketing.
I'm curious a what are those specializations that are highest value today that are very Attractive for someone like us, you'd imagine.
And then B, who does it actually take at the.
Let's assume we're going in a structure where that we keep the agency team in place for the most part because we're happy with their performance.
But we do have some kind of senior leadership leading the brands the complete portfolio.
Like so what are those agencies specializing in that are most desirable?
And then what does this cap the org chart look like of the portfolio level group?
That's like managing, not data the day to day, but managing oversight of those agencies.
Who do you need in leadership at the portfolio level?
Yeah, so there are a couple of categories that do really well.
Influencer marketing is, is one category in particular that does well but it does tend to have a bit of SaaS in there.
So they're more expensive.
But not all of them do.
Some of them are just managing influencer campaigns without any of that.
And then like I said, there's account based management firms that are also extremely valuable.
And then besides that, I would say it's the more traditional firms or ones that tend to do like a broader portfolio of services but they are closer to the strategy side of things.
So they will work directly with the brand.
They will come up with the full marketing strategy across lots of different channels.

And they may be specialists in some of those channels but they could white label stuff from other smaller agencies as well or they do it with freelancers or just on an ad hoc basis to sort of fill out the full service scope that they supply themselves.
So those types of agencies definitely do well.
So yeah, it's kind of really trying to figure out which ones you can get hold of.
And so one of the reasons why we're building the roll ups is because the platform size businesses, they either don't exist or they are going backwards because they're long in the tooth.
And so they've suffered from COVID they've suffered from the riotous strikes, they've suffered from Trump coming into power.
You know they will list out a million different reasons why they're going backwards, but really it's because they haven't updated their methods.
And maybe there is an opportunity in those types of more traditional companies for you.
But generally speaking, private equity or capital wants to go for at least flat or slight growth.
So I guess it's just.
Yeah, no, no, definitely want growth but just can see, you know, they're growing 10% top line, whatever the desired amount is.
But they're losing, you know, they're churning 10% right there.
And so you know, obviously it requires a little bit of hubris, but, you know, the goal is.
Okay, well, you know, it's.
If we believe in our systems and our technology that we're bringing in immediately that 10% becomes 15%.
Right.
Because we're reducing the churn.
So obviously making up numbers and there's a lot of assumptions baked in there.
I've got a couple more questions, but.
Look, hopefully while you've got me on, because I've got another call in seven minutes, then another one in 37.
Yeah, I don't want to, I don't want to talk your ear off.
Look, as you can tell, we are kind of in this information gathering mode.
There's a lot of these that are in our criteria.
I've got a list of them in your, in your, from your sheet.
I'm just pulling it up from your marketplace.
You know, some of them are a little rich for us.
You have one that's at 6x.
I think we'd try and stay below 5x.
And I think there's, you know, there's.
I see a, there's a $6 million valued one, a $5.5 million one, or excuse me, $300,000 one.
That's obviously going to be a little light.
The.
There's a 3.6, $850,000 one.
I mean, I'm happy to look at all them.
I don't know if these are firm prices that you think the sellers typically stick at or if they're room for negotiation.
All the.
I've got 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 that are interesting.
I don't know if that's all the NDAs I filled out, but yeah, I would love to take a look at the Sims because I think we're ready to kind of pull the trigger here in the next 60 days or so.
And you know, I don't know typically the timelines you guys work on with.
The sell side clients, but yeah, the quicker the better.
So we've got a few in there.
So Project Pax, Wonder, Reptile and Corinthia.
I'll send you those for.
I think some of the others might be older ones and we're gonna have to go back and check whether they're still available.
They've just come up with not set project titles, just three of them.
So.
But certainly the other three, four we'll be able to take a look at.
So our process is we go back to our clients and obviously if there's no reason for them not to want to share it, we will Share it.
So we just double check with the client.
So I think we just take this on our recommendation.
So understanding that you're pulling the trigger in 60, within 60 days on one of, one of these then I would be happy to.
I guess I should, I guess I should clarify 60 days probably before pulling the trigger on a letter of an indication of interest, you know and then starting diligent.
The whole transaction closing is probably going to take a little longer but yeah, sure.
Yeah sure.
So just in terms of the timelines for these, some are more suitable than others, so perfect.
So yeah, I mean obviously for my education edification, the more the merrier.
But yeah, obviously don't want to waste any of the people's times if they're further along in diligence with other buyers or whatever the case may be.
Yeah, exactly.
But look, let's stay in touch and also I've got some of these roll ups coming together.
I know you're obviously looking for five and under but it may be that I can save you a year, two years of time by pulling some together.
But at least I'll keep you on the list to present.
Yeah, that's appreciated.
No, I'd love to look at those.
It's a really interesting strategy you guys are doing.
Yeah, amazing.
If you do have two minutes, I am excited to get a hold of those sims here shortly and maybe these questions will be answered in them.
Are there any verticals like to specialize in that you've seen agencies at this size really succeed in?
You know, I guess if it's social media influencer, that's going to be more E commerce.
You know we, we've seen there are reasons we like some of the more SMB localized marketing agencies.
So law firms, medical practices, those seem to be big specialties or verticals of different agencies.
Curious your thoughts on one versus the other.
Yeah, I would say the ones that broadly work directly with brands are worth more ultimately.
Obviously you are in a niche of niches once you go down sort of those agencies that specialize in say dental or veterinarian.
But we do see a lot of very large agencies that focus around health, wellness and pharmaceuticals.
So I would certainly say pharmaceuticals seems to be a growing one.
Whether that continues to grow, whether there's a backlash with the current government in the US we'd have to see.
But I think very generally outside of that, like I said those traditional advertising firms, account based marketing and the ones with like broad services, they do tend to be valued better.

So like you say, if you can get up to 10 million EBITDA, then you're looking at double digits, particularly for account based marketing, growth marketing and those sort of more traditional advertising or full service marketing.
Yeah, I mean.
All right, Andy, I'll let you go.
Yeah, you could send over those sims at your convenience.
That's really appreciated.
And they'll come from Ahmed.
Are you in touch with Ahmed at all?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, we've been emailing.
I'll let them know.
Yeah, they'll come from Ahmed, so.
So feel free to chase him up for them if you don't get them.
But I will speak to him and make sure he sends you the three or four appropriate.
All right, good stuff.
Or is it Andrew or Andy?
You prefer Andy?
I'm actually.
I am Andy, but the reason why I put Andrew on is because people phone me up constantly and call me Andy and I always feel like I know them.
So I put Andrew on everything.
Now that we know each other, it's nice to meet you.
I'm an Andy.
Amazing.
All right, well, we'll talk very soon.
Thanks so much for your time.
All right, speak.
Speak soon.
Cheers.

summary.overview:
- Philip's firm operates with a unique investment model focused on funding startups and acquiring businesses, adaptable based on market conditions.
- Targeting agencies with $500K-$2M EBITDA, aiming for a combined $2-3M EBITDA across multiple acquisitions for optimal entry.
- Seeking 15-20% EBITDA margins initially, with plans to enhance to 25-35% through operational improvements across acquired agencies.
- Agencies face challenges with low margins, heavy reliance on referrals, and high staff turnover, creating a significant investment opportunity.
- Multi-agency roll-up strategy projected to increase $3M EBITDA to $10M, capturing elevated valuation multiples from grouping.
- Solo agencies typically sell for ~5x EBITDA, while those in clusters can achieve 8-9x, emphasizing the value in strategic aggregation.
- Current operational inefficiencies identified in sales processes, highlighting the need to separate business development from account management to enhance retention.
- Influencer marketing and account-based marketing agencies show high value, while health/wellness sectors indicate strong growth potential.
- Seven promising opportunities identified in Andy's marketplace, with Philip targeting a letter of intent within the next 60 days.
- Follow-up on several specific projects, including Project Pax and Wonder, to maintain momentum and explore deal pipeline effectively.
summary.short_summary: Philip's firm utilizes a distinctive investment model aimed at funding startups and acquiring businesses, particularly targeting agencies with EBITDA between $500K and $2M. The goal is to achieve a combined EBITDA of $2-3M across multiple acquisitions, initially seeking 15-20% margins, with plans to improve these to 25-35% through operational enhancements. Challenges faced by agencies, such as low margins and high staff turnover, present significant investment opportunities. The multi-agency roll-up strategy is expected to increase EBITDA from $3M to $10M, capitalizing on higher valuation multiples. Solo agencies typically sell for about 5x EBITDA, while clustered agencies can achieve 8-9x. Operational inefficiencies in sales processes highlight the need for separation between business development and account management. Philip has identified seven promising opportunities and aims for a letter of intent within 60 days, while also following up on specific projects.
